english: to throb / for one's heart to pound (with excitement or nerves)
usage: The default subject is 가슴(이) or 심장(이) — the heart, never the person. Say 가슴이 두근거려요, not 저는 두근거려요.
to go thump-thump / be all aflutter
The mimetic root 두근두근 also works as its own verb 두근두근하다, and the bare 두근두근 floods captions and texts.
Pairing it with 설레서 locks in the happy reading; pairing it with 긴장돼서 forces the nervous reading instead.
enough to make your heart race
A natural intensifier slot — 두근거릴 만큼 설레는 / 무서운 means 'thrillingly ~' or 'scarily ~.'
examples: 가슴이 두근두근해요.
My heart is going thump-thump.
The simplest form: the mimetic 두근두근 + 하다. Kids and adults both say this.
발표 직전이라 심장이 두근거려요.
It's right before my presentation, so my heart is racing.
심장이 두근거리다 and 가슴이 두근거리다 are interchangeable; 가슴 sounds a touch softer and more everyday.
내일 그 사람 만난다고 생각하니까 벌써 두근거려.
Just thinking about meeting them tomorrow, my heart's already fluttering.
Casual 두근거려 to a close friend, with the subject 가슴 left unspoken because context makes it obvious.
nuance: 두근거리다 names the physical sensation of a pounding, fluttering heartbeat, built from the mimetic 두근 ('thump') + the repetitive-motion suffix -거리다, so its grammatical subject is 가슴/심장 and the person is marked with -은/는 or a cause phrase, never as the doer. It spans the whole range from giddy anticipation to dread, so Koreans lean on partners — 설레서 두근거리다 for good nerves, 긴장돼서 두근거리다 for bad — to pin down which. Its close cousin 떨리다 also means 'tremble/be nervous' but centres on shakiness rather than the heartbeat itself, and 설레다 names the emotion while 두근거리다 names the bodily symptom of it. The English-speaker trap is treating it like 'I'm excited' and saying 저는 두근거려요; let the heart be the subject (가슴이 두근거려요), or switch to 저는 설레요 when you mean the feeling.

english: to miss / to long for (someone or something absent)
usage: 그립다 is an adjective, so what you miss takes -이/가, not -을/를: 고향이 그리워요, never 고향을 그리워요.
a person one misses / a dear, longed-for face
그리운 + noun is the natural modifier: 그리운 얼굴, 그리운 옛날 — wistful, slightly literary.
To report a third person's longing, switch to the verb 그리워하다, which CAN take -을/를: 동생이 고향을 그리워해요.
사무치게 ('piercingly, to the bone') is the set intensifier for deep, painful longing in songs and writing.
examples: 고향이 그리워요.
I miss my hometown.
The base pattern: the thing missed takes -이/가, and ㅂ-irregular 그립- + -어요 gives 그리워요.
한국에 산 지 일 년 됐는데 가끔 엄마 음식이 그리워요.
It's been a year living in Korea, and sometimes I miss my mom's cooking.
Everyday expat use; you can long for food and places, not only people.
친구가 너무 그리워서 영상통화를 했어.
I missed my friend so much that I made a video call.
그리워서 (because I missed) drives a real action. To say someone else actively misses, you'd switch to 그리워하다.
nuance: 그립다 is an adjective expressing your own felt longing, so the thing you miss is the subject (-이/가) and you cannot hang a direct object on it; to describe a third person missing something ('he misses home') Korean shifts to the verb 그리워하다, because Korean treats adjectives of feeling as reportable only from the inside. The sharp contrast to learn is 보고 싶다 vs 그립다: 보고 싶다 ('want to see') is the everyday, conversational way to say you miss a specific person and works fine for texting a friend, whereas 그립다 is more wistful, broader (it covers places, eras, tastes, not just faces), and reads as faintly literary. It's a ㅂ-irregular, so the ㅂ turns to 우 before vowel endings: 그립- + -어요 → 그리워요, past 그리웠어요. The classic English trap is the object particle — 'I miss my hometown' tempts you to say 고향을 그리워요, but the correct adjective frame is 고향이 그리워요.

Defaulting to 그립다 when texting a friend 'I miss you' — Koreans say 보고 싶어, which is warmer and more direct than the wistful 그립다.

english: to be embarrassed / to be shy / to be ashamed
usage: The textbook physical tell: 부끄러워서 + 얼굴이 빨개지다 ('face goes red') is the stock collocation.
to act shy / be bashful (of others)
Use the verb 부끄러워하다 to describe someone else's shyness or to tell them not to be shy: 부끄러워하지 마세요.
부끄러운 줄 알다 ('to know to be ashamed') is a fixed scolding phrase — here the sense is moral shame, not shyness.
부끄럼(을) 타다 (also 수줍음을 타다) describes a temperament — being naturally bashful around people.
examples: 저는 좀 부끄러워요.
I'm a little shy.
The base feeling about oneself; ㅂ-irregular 부끄럽- + -어요 → 부끄러워요.
사람들 앞에서 한국어로 말하는 게 아직 부끄러워요.
I'm still shy about speaking Korean in front of people.
The cause (말하는 게) takes -이/가 because this is an adjective describing your own state.
동생이 낯선 사람을 부끄러워해요.
My younger sibling is shy around strangers.
For someone else's shyness, switch to the verb 부끄러워하다, which can take an object (낯선 사람을).
nuance: 부끄럽다 covers both bashful shyness (meeting new people, being praised) and self-conscious embarrassment over a small slip, and it leans gentler, more inward and even endearing compared with 창피하다, which is sharper, louder, public mortification. The dividing line worth memorising: 부끄럽다 ≈ shy/quietly abashed and can sound cute, while 창피하다 ≈ 'I want to disappear' after a public blunder; a child hiding behind a parent is 부끄러워하는 것, not 창피해하는 것. Because it's an adjective, your own feeling and its cause take -이/가, and reporting someone else's shyness requires the verb 부끄러워하다 (third-person feelings need the -어하다 verb across this whole word family). It's a ㅂ-irregular: 부끄럽- + -어요 → 부끄러워요, past 부끄러웠어요. The related noun 부끄러움 ('shyness/shame') belongs to more formal or written registers. English speakers often grab 부끄럽다 for strong public humiliation — for that punch, reach for 창피하다 instead.

Forgetting the ㅂ-irregular and saying 부끄럽어요; the ㅂ becomes 우, giving 부끄러워요.

english: to be embarrassing / to feel mortified
usage: -아/어 죽겠다 ('dying of ~') is the go-to intensifier with feeling words; 창피해 죽겠어요 is extremely common.
to be humiliated / put to shame
The noun 창피(를) 당하다 frames it as something inflicted on you in public — a stronger, more formal phrasing.
창피한 줄(도) 모르다 ('not even know to be embarrassed') criticizes shamelessness — a common cutting remark.
to be embarrassing in front of others
남(이) 보기에 + 창피하다, or the compound 남부끄럽다, foregrounds shame specifically about how others see you.
examples: 아, 진짜 창피해.
Ugh, this is so embarrassing.
The blunt casual reaction. 하다-verb contracts: 창피하- + -아 → 창피해.
사람들이 다 쳐다봐서 창피했어요.
Everyone was staring, so I was embarrassed.
Past 창피했어요; the cause here is a public situation, which is typical of this word.
그렇게 큰 소리로 말하면 내가 창피하잖아.
If you talk that loudly, you embarrass me.
Used to tell someone they're embarrassing you; -잖아 adds a mild complaining, 'come on' tone.
nuance: 창피하다 is the stronger, more public sibling of 부끄럽다 — the 'I want the floor to swallow me' feeling after you trip in a crowd or get scolded openly — and it describes either your own mortification (저 창피해요) or the situation that causes it (창피한 상황). It is Sino-Korean: 창피 猖披, where 猖 means 'run wild/rampage' and 披 means 'spread open, be dishevelled,' the image being clothes worn so carelessly you're exposed, hence ashamed. The three-way register map is worth holding: 부끄럽다 = gentle/shy, 창피하다 = strong public embarrassment (neutral-polite), and 쪽팔리다 = the same feeling but slangy, rough, friends-only and unfit for work or elders. As a 하다-adjective it contracts 창피하- + -아요 → 창피해요 (not 창피하아요), past 창피했어요. The English-speaker pitfall is reaching for the slang 쪽팔리다 in a workplace or with seniors to sound natural — keep 창피하다 there, since 쪽팔리다 can read as crude.

Using 창피하다 for mild bashful shyness (e.g., a child meeting a guest) — that gentler feeling is 부끄럽다.

english: to be absurd / to be dumbfounded by something ridiculous
usage: 황당한 + noun describes the baffling thing itself: 황당한 일, 황당한 상황, 황당한 변명, 황당한 소문.
황당한 표정(을) 짓다 / 황당한 표정으로 쳐다보다 is a set phrase for the stunned face you make.
-기 짝이 없다 ('beyond compare ~') is a slightly formal intensifier: 황당하기 짝이 없는 일.
to be both flabbergasted and baffled
Koreans often stack it with 어이없다 for emphasis, since the two overlap but aren't identical.
examples: 진짜 황당해요.
This is honestly ridiculous.
The base reaction. 하다-verb: 황당하- + -아요 → 황당해요.
갑자기 예약이 취소됐다고 해서 너무 황당했어요.
They suddenly said my reservation was canceled, so I was dumbfounded.
Past 황당했어요; a very common customer-service mishap context.
그 사람 변명이 너무 황당해서 웃음이 나왔어.
His excuse was so absurd that I burst out laughing.
황당해서 (because it was absurd) leads to a reaction. Casual register with a friend.
nuance: 황당하다 captures the 'wait, what?' feeling when something is so unexpected or illogical that it leaves you stunned — a baffling excuse, an out-of-nowhere cancellation, an absurd demand — and it covers both the ridiculous thing itself (황당한 변명) and your reaction to it (너무 황당했어요). It is Sino-Korean: 황당 荒唐, where 荒 means 'wild/overgrown/desolate' and 唐 carries an old sense of 'boastful, rambling, far-fetched,' so the literal flavour is 'wildly preposterous.' The synonym to separate it from is 어이없다: 황당하다 leans toward 'bizarre/unbelievable, doesn't compute,' while 어이없다 adds exasperation or contempt ('so dumb it's almost offensive'); a UFO story is 황당하다, but a line-cutter is more 어이없다. Don't confuse it with the near-twin 당황하다 ('to panic/be flustered'), which is about losing your own composure, not judging something as absurd. As a 하다-adjective: 황당하- + -아요 → 황당해요, past 황당했어요. The English trap is translating it as plain 'surprised' (놀라다) — 황당하다 specifically implies absurdity, not mere unexpectedness.

english: to be flabbergasted / to find something absurd and senseless
usage: The headword is a contraction of 어이가 없다; the 가 stays in careful speech and drops in fast speech: 어이없어.
어이없는 + noun is the core collocation: 어이없는 변명, 어이없는 상황, 어이없는 실수.
to be too dumbfounded to speak
The stock follow-up: 어이없어서 + 말이 안 나오다 / 헛웃음이 나오다 ('a dry laugh comes out').
Because 없다 acts as an adjective, a third person's reaction uses the verb 어이없어하다: 친구가 어이없어했어요.
examples: 와, 진짜 어이없어.
Wow, this is unbelievable.
The everyday speechless reaction; the 가 of 어이가 없다 drops in casual speech.
새치기를 하길래 진짜 어이없었어요.
Someone cut in line, so I was totally flabbergasted.
없다-type adjective: 어이없- + -었어요 → 어이없었어요. Note -길래 = 'because (I saw/noticed).'
그 말 듣고 너무 어이없어서 헛웃음이 나왔어.
After hearing that, I was so dumbfounded I let out a dry laugh.
Pairs naturally with 헛웃음 (a hollow, dry laugh). Casual register.
nuance: 어이없다 (full form 어이가 없다) is the punchy, everyday way Koreans react to something so absurd, unfair, or stupid that it stuns them into a speechless half-laugh — 어이 means roughly 'the wits/sense' you'd need to handle the situation, so 'lacking 어이' is being knocked clean out of your composure. Set beside 황당하다, it carries more exasperation or contempt: 황당하다 = 'this is bizarre/doesn't compute,' while 어이없다 = 'this is so dumb it almost offends me,' which is why it's what you mutter when someone cuts in line or hands you a nonsense excuse. It's a hair more casual than 황당하다 but still fine in polite speech (어이없어요); the truly rough register would be slang like 어처구니없다's blunt cousins or profanity. Because 없다 behaves like an adjective, a third party's reaction takes the verb 어이없어하다. The most common pitfalls are spelling and polarity: it is 어이없다 (the cute misspelling 어의없다 is wrong), and it is always negative — never use it for a pleasant surprise.

english: to be thrilling / to feel an electric, tingling rush
usage: 짜릿한 + noun is the engine: 짜릿한 순간, 짜릿한 경기 (a nail-biter), 짜릿한 역전승 (a thrilling comeback win).
짜릿한 느낌 / 짜릿한 기분 names the buzz directly; often paired with the loanword 스릴 (thrill).
to tingle and tingle / be electrifying
Doubling the root gives 짜릿짜릿하다, intensifying the repeated tingling jolt — common for cold water or a real shock.
to feel a thrill / a rush
The noun 짜릿함 ('the thrill') appears in 짜릿함을 느끼다 and in ad copy promising an exciting experience.
examples: 우와, 짜릿해!
Whoa, what a rush!
The base exclamation. 하다-verb: 짜릿하- + -아 → 짜릿해.
롤러코스터 탈 때 그 짜릿한 느낌이 좋아.
I love that electric thrill when riding a roller coaster.
짜릿한 느낌/스릴 are natural collocations; casual ending with a friend.
역전골이 터지는 순간 진짜 짜릿했어요.
The moment the comeback goal went in, it was such a rush.
Past 짜릿했어요; sports — especially a last-second turnaround — are the classic context.
nuance: 짜릿하다 originally describes a literal tingling, electric sensation — a mild shock, a cold splash, a limb that's gone numb — and extends to the metaphorical thrill of exhilarating moments like a comeback win, a thrill ride, or a daring success; it's overwhelmingly positive and high-adrenaline. The synonym to contrast is 신나다: 신나다 is broad, upbeat 'fun/psyched' (a party, a good song), whereas 짜릿하다 is the sharp, spine-tingling spike of intensity, so a fun picnic is 신나다 but a buzzer-beater is 짜릿하다; it also outranks calm 재미있다 ('enjoyable'). It frequently teams up with the loanword 스릴 (짜릿한 스릴) and powers marketing copy for rides, sports, and games. As a 하다-adjective it contracts 짜릿하- + -아요 → 짜릿해요, past 짜릿했어요. Two pitfalls for English speakers: don't downgrade it to ordinary mild fun (use 재미있다/신나다 for calmer enjoyment), and watch the spelling — it has a double ㅈ (ㅉ) and a tense ㅌ, so it's 짜릿하다, not 자릿하다.

english: to feel hurt / to feel let down by someone close
usage: please don't take it the wrong way
A set phrase to reassure someone you didn't mean to slight them; 섭섭하게 생각하다 = 'to take it as a snub.'
섭섭한 + noun: 섭섭한 마음, 섭섭한 감정 — the soft letdown you carry, often voiced gently.
섭섭하다's closest synonym; the two are largely interchangeable, 서운하다 sounding a touch softer and more current.
To report a third person's hurt, use the verb 섭섭해하다: 친구가 섭섭해하더라고요.
examples: 조금 섭섭해요.
I'm a little hurt.
The base feeling, kept soft with 조금. 하다-verb: 섭섭하- + -아요 → 섭섭해요.
생일인데 연락도 안 해서 좀 섭섭했어요.
It was my birthday and you didn't even text, so I felt a bit hurt.
Past 섭섭했어요; the classic mild-grievance use, never rising to real anger.
벌써 간다니까 섭섭하네요.
Hearing you're already leaving makes me sad to see you go.
The bittersweet-goodbye sense, not grievance at all. -네요 adds soft, freshly-felt emotion.
nuance: 섭섭하다 is a uniquely Korean shade of feeling: a gentle, wistful hurt or letdown when someone close doesn't meet your emotional expectations, or the bittersweet pang of parting. The near-synonym 서운하다 sits almost on top of it — most speakers use them interchangeably — with 섭섭하다 carrying a slightly older, warmer texture and 서운하다 feeling a touch softer and more current; both are far milder than anger, so they are wrong for 화나다 ('be angry') or 짜증나다 ('be annoyed/irritated'). The whole point of saying 섭섭해 is social: it signals 'you let me down a little' and invites reassurance rather than confrontation, which is exactly why the reply 섭섭하게 생각하지 마 ('don't take it the wrong way') is so common. As a 하다-adjective it contracts 섭섭하- + -아요 → 섭섭해요, and a third person's hurt takes the verb 섭섭해하다. The key English-speaker pitfall is treating it as anger or using it about strangers — it presumes a relationship close enough to have expectations in the first place.

english: to be sick of / to get fed up with something
usage: The source of your boredom takes -에 (most standard) or -이/가: 라면에 질렸어요 / 라면이 질렸어요.
to the point of getting sick of it
질릴 만큼 ('enough to tire of it') is a common 'way too much' intensifier: 질릴 만큼 먹었어요.
A wholly separate sense: 겁에 질리다 / 공포에 질리다 = frozen with fear, not bored. Same verb, different world.
새파랗게 질리다 / 얼굴이 질리다 = to go white in the face from shock or fear — the 'turn pale' meaning.
examples: 이제 질렸어요.
I'm sick of it now.
The base 'fed up' statement; 이-stem 질리- + -었어요 → 질렸어요.
매일 라면만 먹으니까 이제 진짜 질렸어요.
Eating only ramen every day, I'm really sick of it now.
The source is marked with -에 (라면에) as the textbook choice; everyday over-saturation.
그 말 듣고 겁에 질려서 아무 말도 못 했어요.
Hearing that, I froze in fear and couldn't say a word.
The other meaning entirely: 겁에 질리다 = paralyzed with fear. Context tells the two senses apart.
nuance: 질리다 is the everyday verb for being so over-saturated with something — a food, a routine, a song — that you can't stand a drop more of it, the 'I'm so done with this' feeling; for this sense you mark the source with -에 (most standard) or -이/가, and the partner phrases 질릴 만큼 / 질릴 정도 mean 'to the point of being fed up.' But it has a second, scarier life: 질리다 also means to turn pale or be paralyzed with fear, as in 겁에 질리다 ('frozen with terror') and 새파랗게 질리다 ('go deathly white'), so context decides which world you're in. Compared with 지겹다 ('tedious, dragging on and boring you'), 질리다 stresses saturation from too much of a thing rather than slow tedium, and unlike 싫증 나다 ('lose interest') it can hit a sharp 'can't take it' wall. The recurring English trap is the particle: 'I'm sick of ramen' tempts 라면을 질렸어요, but the correct marker is -에 (라면에 질렸어요) or -이/가, never -을/를.

english: to be excited / to feel one's heart flutter with anticipation
usage: The natural subject is 마음/가슴: 마음이 설레요. The cause comes via a -에/생각에 phrase, e.g. 여행 생각에 설레요.
설레는 + noun (마음, 기분) is a hugely common collocation for happy anticipation: 설레는 마음으로 기다리다.
The noun 설렘 — NOT 설레임 — floods song lyrics and captions: 첫 만남의 설렘 ('the flutter of a first meeting').
to jump the gun / get ahead of oneself
A false friend: 설레발(을) 치다 is unrelated in meaning (acting prematurely), so don't assume it's the verb of 설렘.
examples: 너무 설레요.
I'm so excited / my heart's all aflutter.
The base feeling; 설레- + -어요 contracts to 설레요.
내일 여행 가는 생각에 벌써 설레요.
Just thinking about the trip tomorrow, I'm already giddy.
The cause rides on 생각에 ('at the thought of'); note the standard form is 설레다, not 설레이다.
첫 데이트라서 너무 설렜어요.
It was a first date, so my heart was really fluttering.
Past 설렜어요 (설레 + 었 → 설렜); one of the most-loved feeling words in K-dramas.
nuance: 설레다 is the warm, fluttery thrill of looking forward to something good — the butterflies before a date, a trip, or a fresh start — and it names the emotion itself, with 마음/가슴 as the typical subject. The contrast students need is 설레다 vs 긴장되다: both quicken the heart, but 설레다 is sweet, hopeful anticipation while 긴장되다 ('get nervous/tense') is anxious pressure, so a first date can be both 설레고 긴장돼요; meanwhile 두근거리다 names the bodily pounding that 설레다 produces. The single most important accuracy point is the form: the standard dictionary verb is 설레다 (present 설레요, past 설렜어요, noun 설렘), and although you will see 설레이다 / 설레여요 / 설레임 absolutely everywhere in lyrics and posts, those are nonstandard — write 설레요 / 설렜어요 / 설렘. The English-speaker pitfall is exactly that: copying the pretty but incorrect 설레임 from a caption, and mis-contracting the past as 설레었어요 instead of the natural 설렜어요.

english: to be giddy / to get keyed up with restless excitement
usage: for one's mood to lift / get giddy
The subject is usually 마음/기분: 마음이 들떴어요 — a buzzy lift before something fun.
들뜬 + noun: 들뜬 마음, 들뜬 분위기, 들뜬 목소리 — a giddy mood, like a Friday night out.
to be in a keyed-up state
들떠 있다 describes an ongoing giddy state: 다들 들떠 있어요 ('everyone's all hyped').
들뜨지 말다 is a stock gentle caution — a reminder not to lose your head in the excitement.
examples: 벌써부터 마음이 들떠요.
My heart's already getting giddy.
The base feeling; ㅡ-irregular 들뜨- + -어요 → 들떠요.
연휴라서 그런지 마음이 들떴어요.
Maybe because it's a long weekend, I felt giddy and restless.
Past 들떴어요 (들뜨 + 었 → 들떴); the cause is often a holiday or event.
너무 들뜨지 말고 짐부터 챙기자.
Don't get too carried away — let's pack first.
들뜨지 말다 ('don't get over-excited'), a gentle reminder to stay grounded.
nuance: 들뜨다 is the bubbly, restless excitement that lifts your mood before something fun, literally formed from 들- ('rise up') + 뜨다 ('float'), so the image is your spirits floating up off the ground. That picture explains its faint undertone: you're so giddy you're a little distracted or unsettled, which is exactly why 너무 들뜨지 마 ('don't get carried away') is such a common caution. Against 설레다 (sweet, inward heart-fluttering anticipation), 들뜨다 is more buzzy, outward and hyped — and can shade slightly negative (over-excited, not thinking straight), whereas 설레다 stays purely lovely; it's also more restless than the simple high spirits of 신나다. It conjugates as a ㅡ-irregular: when a vowel ending follows, the ㅡ drops, so 들뜨- + -어 → 들떠 (요), past 들떴어요, and before -ㅂ니다 you get 들뜹니다. The English-speaker pitfalls are botching that ㅡ-drop (saying 들뜨어요 instead of 들떠요) and assuming it's purely positive when it can quietly imply 'overexcited.'

english: to be intimidated / to feel cowed and shrink back
usage: for one's spirit to shrink (full form)
The compound comes from 주눅(이) 들다, so you'll also see the particle kept: 주눅이 들었어요.
to be cowed by the atmosphere
The cause takes -에: 분위기에, 사람들 앞에서 주눅들다 — to feel small in a tense, high-pressure setting.
don't shrink back / don't be cowed
Almost always encouragement; 주눅들지 마(세요) is the standard pep-talk line.
The natural opposite to pair it with: 주눅들지 말고 당당하게 ('don't be cowed — be confident').
examples: 저는 쉽게 주눅들어요.
I get intimidated easily.
The base statement about a tendency; 주눅들- + -어요 → 주눅들어요.
한국어 실력이 부족해서 회의 때 자꾸 주눅들어요.
My Korean isn't good enough, so I keep getting cowed in meetings.
A very real expat workplace feeling; note formal 주눅듭니다 drops the ㄹ before -ㅂ니다.
주눅들지 말고 당당하게 말해.
Don't shrink back — speak up confidently.
주눅들지 말다 paired with 당당하게 ('confidently'), the opposite attitude. A common pep-talk.
nuance: 주눅들다 (from 주눅(이) 들다, where 주눅 is the native noun for 'cowed timidity' and 들다 means 'to set in') means to feel so intimidated or self-conscious that you shrink back, lose your nerve, and can't assert yourself — a genuinely useful word for the expat experience of freezing up in Korean meetings or formal settings. Set it against 긴장하다 ('get nervous/tense'): 긴장하다 is momentary jitters before a test or speech and is neutral, whereas 주눅들다 is a deflating loss of confidence that makes you cower and stay small, often before someone or something more powerful; it's also more passive and lasting than a quick 당황하다 ('fluster'). It's built on 들다, so it follows the ㄹ-irregular pattern — the ㄹ drops before ㅂ/ㄴ/ㅅ endings, giving 주눅듭니다 (not 주눅들습니다) — while vowel endings keep it: 주눅들어요, past 주눅들었어요. The natural cure-words are 당당하다 ('be self-assured') and the encouragement 주눅들지 마. English-speaker pitfalls: keeping the ㄹ before -ㅂ니다, and marking the cause with -을/를 instead of the correct -에 (분위기에 주눅들다).
